c.tagline: Colonial silver-mining city beneath the legendary Cerro Rico, one of the highest cities on Earth.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree a price before departure. Shared 'trufis' running fixed routes are the cheapest way to get around.

emergency.note: Response times can be slow at this altitude; for serious issues go directly to a private clinic and contact your embassy.

avoid.reason: Silver-mine tours carry real hazards (explosives, gas, tight tunnels) — use reputable operators only

hood_desc: The colonial core of Potosí, a UNESCO World Heritage Site built on silver wealth, packed with baroque churches, balconied mansions, and the Casa de la Moneda mint museum.
A quieter colonial quarter around the Convento de San Francisco, known for rooftop views over the city's red-tiled roofs to Cerro Rico.
The mining district at the foot of the legendary 'mountain that eats men,' where cooperative miners still work largely by hand; guided (and physically demanding) mine tours start from here.
A working-class residential neighborhood with a strong local feel, well away from the tourist circuit.
Potosí's central market area, crowded with stalls selling produce, coca leaves, and household goods; a good spot for cheap local food.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water; the altitude also warrants extra hydration care.

transit.map: No official transit map; routes are fixed but informal
transit.note: No metro; trufis and micros cover the city cheaply, and the compact historic center is very walkable (altitude permitting).

bus: Long-distance buses connect Potosí to Sucre (about 3 hours), La Paz (about 10 hours), and Uyuni (about 3-4 hours)

tip.r: Tipping isn't customary but rounding up or leaving small change is appreciated; mine-tour guides usually expect a modest tip.

landmarks: Cerro Rico
The Rich Hill that bankrolled the Spanish Empire looms rust-red over the city, honeycombed with five centuries of silver mining tunnels.
Casa Nacional de la Moneda
This fortress-like colonial Royal Mint, among the Americas' finest museums, displays giant mule-driven coining machines and the enigmatic grinning mask of Bacchus.
Convento de San Francisco
Bolivia's oldest monastery offers catacomb tours and a rooftop walk with the classic postcard panorama of Cerro Rico rising over tiled roofs.
Torre de la Compania de Jesus
All that remains of the Jesuit church, this lavish mestizo-baroque bell tower doubles as a viewpoint over Potosi's terracotta rooftops.
Convento-Museo Santa Teresa
A haunting tour of this 1685 Carmelite convent reveals the cloistered lives of wealthy families' daughters amid gilded altars and colonial paintings.
Iglesia de San Lorenzo de Carangas
Its riotously carved mestizo-baroque portal, where indigenous sirens and angels swirl in stone, is the masterpiece symbol of Andean colonial art.
Catedral Basilica de Potosi
The elegant neoclassical cathedral rewards visitors who climb its bell towers with views across the imperial city to the flanks of Cerro Rico.
Plaza 10 de Noviembre
Potosi's arcaded main square, framed by the cathedral and colonial government buildings, is the social heart of one of the world's highest cities.
Arco de Cobija
A whitewashed colonial archway spanning a steep cobbled street once marked the divide between the Spanish city and the indigenous miners' quarters.
Ojo del Inca (Tarapaya)
A perfectly circular volcanic crater lake steams at bath temperature half an hour from town, where the Inca Huayna Capac reputedly soaked.

train.note: No scheduled passenger train serves Potosi. The Rio Mulatos - Potosi line still reaches the city and continues towards Sucre, but it carries freight and occasional specials only. The nearest railhead with regular passenger services is Uyuni, 3-4 hours away by bus, where Empresa Ferroviaria Andina (https://www.fca.com.bo/) runs the Expreso del Sur and Wara Wara del Sur north to Oruro and south through Atocha and Tupiza to Villazon on the Argentine border. Even there the timetable is only a few departures a week and the Expreso is much more comfortable than the Wara Wara, so book seats a day or two ahead at the Uyuni station.

intl.to: Villazon for La Quiaca (Argentina) - continue on foot across the border and pick up Argentine coaches, about 8 hr from Potosi
intl.op: Terminal de Buses Potosi operators — tickets at the terminal

intl.to: San Pedro de Atacama & Calama (Chile) - via Uyuni, changing there for the cross-Andean service
intl.op: Terminal de Buses Potosi and Uyuni operators — tickets at the terminal

bus.note: The Terminal de Buses is on Avenida Las Banderas about 3 km north of the colonial centre, reached by micro or a cheap taxi, and there is a small terminal-use fee payable before boarding. Sucre is 3-4 hours, Uyuni about 4 hours on a much-improved road, Oruro 5-6 hours and La Paz an overnight run; Trans Copacabana, El Dorado and Trans Emperador are among the better operators. Tickets are generally sold only on the day of travel at the company windows, so arrive by mid-morning for an afternoon departure. Nothing runs across a border directly - for Argentina you take a bus to Villazon and walk into La Quiaca, and for Chile you change at Uyuni.

ferry.note: Potosi is landlocked, sits at over 4,000 m in the Bolivian altiplano and has no navigable river or lake, so there is no passenger boat service of any kind.

half.name: Laguna de Kari Kari
half.blurb: Chain of colonial-era reservoirs in the highlands above the city, built to power Cerro Rico's silver mills, now sits amid quiet Andean scenery.

full.name: Sucre
full.blurb: Bolivia's constitutional capital, about three hours away, is a whitewashed colonial city with dinosaur footprints preserved at a nearby quarry.

full.name: Salar de Uyuni
full.blurb: World's largest salt flat, about four hours south, creates a mirror-like surface during the wet season across thousands of square kilometers of white crust.
